nameStory: The redbreast sunfish gets its name from the beautiful reddish-orange coloration that spreads across its chest and belly, especially during breeding season when males show off their most vibrant colors. The scientific name 'auritus' means 'big-eared' in Latin, referring to the prominent dark flap that extends from behind each gill cover like a little ear.
description: The redbreast sunfish is a colorful, disc-shaped freshwater fish that's built like a living dinner plate turned on its side. These feisty little fighters typically grow to about 6-8 inches long, though some can reach up to a foot. Their bodies are laterally compressed (flattened side to side) with a distinctive reddish-orange breast and belly that gives them their common name. Like other sunfish, they have spiny dorsal fins and are popular with anglers as scrappy panfish.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Look for the telltale reddish-orange breast and belly that feels warm to the touch when you handle a fresh catch, contrasting with olive-green to bronze sides

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Deep, disc-like body that's flattened from side to side, feeling solid and muscular when held, similar to holding a small oval dinner plate

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Long, dark ear flap (opercular flap) extending well behind the gill cover, soft to touch and distinctively black without the bright border seen on pumpkinseeds

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small, terminal mouth positioned at the front tip of the head, perfect for picking insects and small invertebrates from vegetation

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Typically 6-8 inches long and palm-sized, though larger specimens up to 12 inches feel surprisingly hefty for their length

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in vegetated areas of lakes and slow-moving streams where they can dart quickly between plants, preferring rocky or structured areas near cover

habitat: Redbreast sunfish thrive in the vegetated shallows and rocky margins of New England's lakes, ponds, and slow-moving rivers. They love areas with plenty of aquatic plants, fallen logs, or rocky structures where they can hunt for insects, snails, and small invertebrates. Look for them in the Connecticut River system and other major watersheds, especially in areas where the water is clear enough for them to spot their tiny prey.

seasonality.spring: Males develop their most intense reddish-orange breeding colors and can be found in shallow areas building circular nests in sandy or gravelly bottoms. This is when their colors are most dramatic and identification is easiest.
seasonality.summer: Active in vegetated shallows during cooler morning and evening hours, feeding heavily on insects and small invertebrates. Colors remain vibrant but may be slightly less intense than peak breeding season.
seasonality.fall: Still active and feeding before winter, though colors begin to fade slightly. They start moving to deeper water as temperatures drop but can still be found near structure.
seasonality.winter: More willing than bluegills to strike moving lures and flies in cold water, making them a favorite target for ice fishermen and winter fly anglers in southern New England waters that don't freeze.

funFact: Male redbreast sunfish are dedicated dads who build perfectly circular nests by fanning away debris with their tails, then guard up to 1,000 eggs and the baby fish for weeks, aggressively chasing away anything that comes too close - even fish many times their size!
confusionNotes: Most often confused with pumpkinseed sunfish, but redbreasts lack the bright orange or red border on their ear flap - theirs is solid dark. Memory trick: 'Redbreast, dark ear; Pumpkinseed, bright ear.' Bluegills have shorter, more rounded ear flaps and lack the intense reddish breast coloration.
compareHints: Compared to its sunfish cousins, the redbreast has the most prominent reddish-orange coloration on its underside and the longest, darkest ear flap without bright borders. Bluegills are more silvery-blue with shorter ear flaps, while pumpkinseeds have colorful orange-red ear flap borders and more mottled sides. Green sunfish have larger mouths and are more uniformly greenish, while warmouth have a more bass-like appearance with bigger mouths and teeth.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's sunfish family, bluegills are distinguished by their prominent blue gill covers and larger mouths compared to pumpkinseeds, lack the long ear flaps of redbreast sunfish, and have a more rounded body shape than the elongated green sunfish.
Among New England's sunfish, pumpkinseeds are the only ones with that signature bright orange-red ear flap.
Green sunfish have a much larger mouth than their sunfish cousins - bigger than bluegills, pumpkinseeds, or redbreast sunfish.
Unlike bluegill and pumpkinseed with their bright colors and small mouths, warmouth are drab and big-mouthed.
